title: Infrastructure as Code with Bicep (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain why infrastructure as code matters and how declarative deployments differ from imperative scripts.
- Compare ARM JSON templates, Bicep and Terraform, and choose one for a team.
- Read and write a Bicep file: parameters, variables, resources, symbolic names, dependencies, outputs, modules, loops, conditions and decorators.
- Deploy safely with scopes, modes and what-if, and protect what you deployed with template specs and deployment stacks — the replacement for Azure Blueprints.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Nineteen lunches in, Nusantara Retail's Azure estate is real — and it was built one portal click and one CLI command at a time. On Tuesday Dewi asks for "a copy of the storefront network for testing". Nobody can produce one that matches. On Wednesday Pak Budi notices an NSG rule he never approved; the activity log says Rizky changed it at 23:00, but not why. On Thursday Ibu Sari reads the disaster recovery notes from Lunch 17 and asks the question that silences the meeting: "If Southeast Asia disappeared tomorrow, could we rebuild everything — exactly the same — in another region, in an hour?"

The honest answer is no. Not because Azure can't, but because the design lives in people's memories instead of in a file.

Today's question: how do you describe Nusantara Retail's Azure environment in code that you can review, repeat and protect?

Reading

1. Why infrastructure as code

Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing your infrastructure — networks, servers, databases, policies — in text files that live next to your application code. You store them in Git, review changes in pull requests and let a tool deploy them. It sounds like a developer's hobby. It is actually an operations and governance practice, and it solves the exact problems Nusantara Retail ran into:

- Repeatability. The test network and the production network come from the same file with different parameters, so "works in test" means something.
- Review and audit. A change to an NSG rule is a pull request that Pak Budi approves before it reaches Azure, and Git history records who changed what, when and why.
- Speed of recovery. Rebuilding an environment is one command, not a weekend with screenshots — the missing piece in the disaster recovery plan from Lunch 17.
- Drift detection. When someone changes a resource by hand, the next preview shows the difference from the file.
- Cheaper experiments. If you can rebuild in minutes, you can delete without fear — the cost habit from Lunch 19.

There are two styles of automation. An imperative script describes how: create the virtual network, then the subnet, then attach the NSG — and if the subnet already exists, handle that error yourself. The Azure CLI scripts in the earlier labs are imperative. A declarative file describes what: "there is a virtual network with these two subnets and this NSG". The engine compares that desired state with what exists and works out the steps. Declarative deployments are idempotent: run the same file twice and the second run changes nothing, because reality already matches.

Every road leads to the same place. Whether you click in the portal, run the CLI or deploy a file, the request goes through Azure Resource Manager (Lunch 04), which checks your permissions and policies and calls the resource providers. IaC simply makes those requests repeatable.

2. ARM templates, Bicep and Terraform

Azure Resource Manager natively understands ARM templates: JSON documents that list parameters, variables, resources and outputs. They are complete and precise, but verbose. Expressions live inside strings in square brackets, such as "[parameters('location')]", and a medium-sized environment quickly becomes hundreds of lines that are hard to review.

Bicep is Microsoft's domain-specific language for the same job. A Bicep file is shorter and reads more like code: you call functions directly, refer to other resources by a symbolic name, and Bicep works out the dependencies. When you deploy, the Bicep CLI transpiles the file into an ARM JSON template, so Bicep can do everything ARM templates can, including every resource type and API version from the day it is released. There is no separate state file: Azure itself is the record of what exists. Bicep is free, open source and supported by Microsoft, and the Visual Studio Code extension gives you IntelliSense, validation and a visualizer.

Terraform, from HashiCorp, is a popular alternative with its own language (HCL). Its strength is reach: one tool and one workflow for Azure, other clouds and many SaaS products. The price of that reach is a state file that records what Terraform manages; you must store it centrally, lock it during changes and protect it, because it can contain secrets.

| ARM templates (JSON) | Bicep | Terraform
Language | JSON with bracket expressions | Concise DSL, compiled to ARM JSON | HCL
Clouds | Azure only | Azure only | Azure, other clouds and SaaS providers
State | Azure is the source of truth | Azure is the source of truth | State file you store, lock and protect
New Azure features | Any API version from day one | Any API version from day one | When the provider supports them (the AzAPI provider can call any API version)
Preview changes | what-if | what-if | terraform plan
Deleting what left the file | Deployment stacks | Deployment stacks | Next apply destroys it
Best fit | Generated or existing templates | Azure-focused teams starting fresh | Multi-cloud teams, existing Terraform skills

For Nusantara Retail — an Azure-only shop with a small team and no existing Terraform code — Bicep is the natural choice. If they later need to manage DNS at another provider or GitHub repositories from the same pipeline, Terraform becomes worth a second look. Both are valid; mixing them for the same resources is not, because two tools that each believe they own a resource will undo each other's changes.

Imperative scripts don't disappear. They remain the right tool for one-off jobs, for data-plane work such as uploading product photos to a container, and as glue inside pipelines: build the Bicep file, run what-if, deploy, then run a short script to smoke-test the result. The rule of thumb is simple: anything that should exist belongs in the declarative file; anything that should happen once can be a script.

Tip: You don't have to start from a blank page. The Export template page of a resource group produces an ARM JSON template of what already exists, and az bicep decompile --file template.json turns JSON into Bicep. Treat the result as a first draft: exported templates contain read-only values and defaults you should delete, and hard-coded names you should turn into parameters.

3. Bicep anatomy

Here is a small but complete Bicep file. It creates a network security group and a virtual network whose subnet uses that NSG:

targetScope = 'resourceGroup'

@description('Azure region for every resource.')
param location string = resourceGroup().location

@allowed([
  'lab'
  'test'
  'prod'
])
param environment string = 'lab'

var tags = {
  costCenter: 'retail-lab'
  environment: environment
}

resource nsgWeb 'Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups@2024-05-01' = {
  name: 'nsg-web'
  location: location
  tags: tags
}

resource vnet 'Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks@2024-05-01' = {
  name: 'vnet-nusa-iac'
  location: location
  tags: tags
  properties: {
    addressSpace: {
      addressPrefixes: [
        '10.20.0.0/16'
      ]
    }
    subnets: [
      {
        name: 'snet-web'
        properties: {
          addressPrefix: '10.20.1.0/24'
          networkSecurityGroup: {
            id: nsgWeb.id // a symbolic reference creates an implicit dependency
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

output vnetId string = vnet.id

Each part has a job:

Element | Syntax | What it is for
Target scope | targetScope = 'resourceGroup' | Where the file deploys: resource group (the default), subscription, management group or tenant
Parameter | param location string = resourceGroup().location | Inputs that change between deployments; defaults can use functions
Decorator | @description(), @allowed(), @minLength(), @secure() | Documentation and validation; @secure() keeps secrets out of logs
Variable | var tags = { … } | A value computed once and reused, such as a tag set
Resource | resource nsgWeb 'Type@apiVersion' = { … } | One Azure resource; the API version fixes which properties exist
Symbolic name | nsgWeb, vnet | How the file refers to a resource — not the Azure name
Implicit dependency | nsgWeb.id used inside vnet | Bicep orders the deployment for you; dependsOn is rarely needed
Existing resource | resource kv '…' existing = { name: '…' } | Refers to a resource the file doesn't deploy
Output | output vnetId string = vnet.id | Values handed back to you or to the next step
Module | module net 'network.bicep' = { params: { … } } | Reuses another Bicep file, locally or from a registry
Loop | [for name in names: { … }] | Many similar resources or properties from an array
Condition | resource logs '…' = if (deployLogs) { … } | Deploys a resource only when an expression is true

The API version in each resource type (@2024-05-01) pins the schema: which properties exist and what they mean. In VS Code, the Bicep extension validates every property against that schema as you type. Functions such as resourceGroup() and uniqueString() help you avoid hard-coded values. uniqueString(resourceGroup().id) returns the same 13-character hash every time for the same resource group, which makes it perfect for globally unique names like storage accounts: unique across Azure, yet identical on every redeploy.

Because vnet refers to nsgWeb.id, Bicep knows the NSG must exist first. Resources that don't depend on each other are created in parallel:

For parameter values, you can type them on the command line or keep them in a .bicepparam file, which starts with using 'main.bicep' and assigns values such as param environment = 'test'. One template plus one parameter file per environment is the classic pattern. Larger codebases add user-defined types, functions and shared files, but the building blocks in the table above take you a long way.

Warning: Never write a password, key or connection string into a Bicep file, a parameter file in Git, or an output. Outputs are stored in the deployment history, where anyone who can read the resource group can see them. Mark secret parameters with @secure(), fetch values from Key Vault at deployment time, and prefer managed identities (Lunch 15) so there is no secret to pass at all.

4. Deploying safely: scopes, modes and what-if

A deployment targets a scope with a matching command: az deployment group create for a resource group, az deployment sub create for a subscription (to create resource groups, policy assignments or budgets), az deployment mg create for a management group and az deployment tenant create for the tenant. Each deployment is itself recorded in Azure, so the resource group's Deployments page shows what was deployed, when and with which parameters.

Resource-group deployments have a mode. Incremental mode, the default and the recommended one, creates or updates what the file describes and leaves everything else in the resource group alone. Complete mode also deletes resources that aren't in the file. Microsoft no longer recommends complete mode and is gradually deprecating it; to delete resources through code, use deployment stacks (section 5).

One subtlety catches almost everyone: the file always describes a resource's complete desired state. If you redeploy an NSG whose file lists one rule, any rule Rizky added by hand disappears, because properties that aren't in the file are reset. That is a feature — the file wins — but only if everyone knows it.

Before anything changes, ask for a preview. What-if compares the file with what exists and prints a diff:

az deployment group what-if --resource-group rg-storefront-test --template-file main.bicep

Each resource gets a symbol: + create, ~ modify (with the changing properties listed underneath), - delete and = no change. In incremental mode you will never see a delete; it appears with complete mode or with a deployment stack that deletes unmanaged resources. What-if sometimes reports noise — properties that Azure filled in with defaults appear as changes even though nothing really changes — so read the diff instead of trusting the summary line. You can also add --confirm-with-what-if to az deployment group create to see the preview and answer yes or no before it deploys.

Problems are cheapest to catch before Azure sees them, so think of three checks that get stricter as they go. az bicep build compiles a file to ARM JSON on your machine and reports errors (a misspelled symbol, a missing brace) and warnings from the built-in linter (an unused parameter, a property the schema doesn't know). Errors stop the build; warnings don't — so read them. Next, az deployment group validate asks Resource Manager whether the template would be accepted in the target resource group, without deploying anything. Finally, what-if shows the actual diff against what exists. By default, what-if checks the same permissions as a real deployment, which is why teams usually let the pipeline's identity run the preview and post the result for reviewers.

Deployments also leave a trail. Give each deployment a meaningful name with --name (otherwise the file name is used), and the resource group's Deployments page keeps the template, the parameters, the outputs and any error for each run. When a deployment fails halfway, fix the file and deploy again: resources that already exist are simply confirmed, and the ones that failed are tried again. That is idempotency paying off.

Finally, a template spec stores a template as a versioned resource in Azure (Microsoft.Resources/templateSpecs). Teams can deploy "network v1.2" from the portal or the CLI without access to your Git repository, and you control who can use it with Azure RBAC.

5. Lifecycle and guardrails: deployment stacks, verified modules and pipelines

A normal deployment creates resources and then forgets about them. A deployment stack (Microsoft.Resources/deploymentStacks) remembers. It deploys a Bicep file or template, keeps a list of the managed resources, and applies two policies to them:

Stack setting | CLI flag | Values | What it does
Action on unmanage | --action-on-unmanage | detachAll, deleteResources, deleteAll | What happens to a resource that leaves the file or when the stack is deleted: keep it as an ordinary unmanaged resource, delete it, or also delete managed resource groups
Deny settings | --deny-settings-mode | none, denyDelete, denyWriteAndDelete | Creates a deny assignment that blocks deletes, or writes and deletes, on managed resources — even for Owners
Exclusions | --deny-settings-excluded-principals, --deny-settings-excluded-actions | Up to 5 principals, up to 200 actions | Exempts, for example, the pipeline's identity or one harmless operation
Child scopes | --deny-settings-apply-to-child-scopes | On or off | Extends the protection to child resources such as SQL databases

Creating one looks like this:

az stack group create --name stack-storefront --resource-group rg-storefront-prod \
  --template-file main.bicep --action-on-unmanage deleteResources \
  --deny-settings-mode denyDelete --yes

Deny settings resemble the resource locks from Lunch 04, with two differences. Locks apply to everyone, including your pipeline; deny settings can exempt named principals. And deny settings travel with the stack: they appear when you deploy it and disappear when you delete it. They protect the control plane only — a DenyDelete stack stops someone deleting the storage account, not deleting a blob inside it — and only resources declared in the file. Creating a stack with deny settings needs extra permissions, which the Azure Deployment Stack Owner role includes. For stronger separation, put the stack at a parent scope (for example, a subscription stack that deploys into a resource group), so people who work in the resource group can't edit the stack itself.

Important: A deny assignment created by a stack belongs to the stack. You can't remove it on the Access control (IAM) page, and being an Owner doesn't help. To change what is protected, update the stack (or delete it). Test deny settings in a lab first, and always exclude the identity that runs your pipeline.

Deployment stacks, together with template specs and Azure Policy, are the recommended replacement for Azure Blueprints, which is being retired: new assignments are blocked from October 31, 2026, and it is fully retired on January 31, 2027.

You don't have to write every resource from scratch. Azure Verified Modules (AVM) is a Microsoft-owned library of tested Bicep and Terraform modules that follow Well-Architected guidance. Resource modules wrap one resource type with sensible, secure defaults; pattern modules combine several. You reference a module from the public registry and pin a version:

module images 'br/public:avm/res/storage/storage-account:<version>' = {
  params: {
    name: 'stnusa${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}'
    skuName: 'Standard_LRS'
  }
}

The last piece is who runs the deployment. In a mature setup, people don't deploy from their laptops: a pipeline does. With GitHub Actions, the workflow asks GitHub for a short-lived OpenID Connect (OIDC) token, and a Microsoft Entra app registration or user-assigned managed identity with a federated credential trusts tokens from that repository and branch. No password or client secret is stored anywhere:

permissions:
  id-token: write   # allow the job to request an OIDC token
  contents: read
steps:
  # (check out the repository first)
  - uses: azure/login@v2
    with:
      client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
      tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
      subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
  - run: az deployment group what-if --resource-group rg-storefront-test --template-file infra/main.bicep

Lunch 22 builds this federated credential step by step.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

The new way of working fits on one page. The repository gets an infra folder: main.bicep, a few modules (network, storage, monitoring) and one .bicepparam file per environment. Dewi's request for a test copy becomes a new parameter file and a pull request. The pipeline runs az bicep build and what-if on every pull request and posts the diff for review. Pak Budi approves network changes in the pull request instead of discovering them in the activity log.

When the pull request merges, the pipeline deploys production as a deployment stack with denyDelete, excluding only the pipeline's own identity. Rizky can still look at everything, but deleting the production storage account by mistake is no longer possible. If Pak Budi wants to stop portal edits as well, denyWriteAndDelete does that, at the cost of making every change go through the pipeline — which is rather the point.

The test environment uses the same files with a different parameter file and the deleteResources action. On Friday evening the team deletes the test stack, and with it every test resource — nothing bills over the weekend. On Monday the pipeline rebuilds it, identical to the tag, in minutes.

And Ibu Sari's question? Rebuilding in another region is now a parameter change plus a deployment, while the data comes back from the backups and replicas you designed in Lunch 17. In Lunch 21 you'll deploy the whole core platform this way, from modular Bicep. Lunch 22 covers the OIDC pipeline identity, and Lunch 31 uses deployment stacks to manage governance across many subscriptions.

Pause and think: at 23:00 Rizky adds an "allow RDP from anywhere" rule to nsg-web in the portal. What happens to that rule the next time the pipeline deploys the Bicep file in incremental mode? And what would have happened at 23:00 if the stack used denyWriteAndDelete and Rizky weren't excluded?

Field notes from Stefanus

A template you have never rebuilt from is only a hope. When someone tells me an environment is "all in Bicep", I ask one question: when did you last delete the test copy and rebuild it from the pipeline alone? The rebuild is the real test, because it finds what the file forgot — a role assignment granted by hand, a secret typed into the portal, a DNS record somebody added late at night. So I schedule that drill, time it, and turn every gap into a pull request. My second habit is smaller: when I review a change, I read the what-if output before the Bicep. The code shows what someone meant; the diff shows what will actually happen, and I look hardest at every - and at any ~ on a resource nobody planned to touch.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: What is Bicep? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/overview) — the language, its benefits and the path from your first file to modules.
- Microsoft Learn: Bicep what-if — preview changes before deployment (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/deploy-what-if) — change types, result formats and how to read the noise.
- Microsoft Learn: Create and deploy Azure deployment stacks in Bicep (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/deployment-stacks) — managed resources, action on unmanage and deny settings with CLI and PowerShell examples.
- Azure Verified Modules — the module index, specifications and how to consume modules in Bicep and Terraform.

quiz.q: Dewi deploys the same Bicep file twice in a row. The second deployment finishes quickly and changes nothing. Which property of declarative infrastructure as code does this show?
quiz.a: Idempotency — why: Resource Manager compares the desired state in the file with what exists and only acts on differences, so repeating a deployment is safe.

quiz.q: You remove the Log Analytics workspace from main.bicep and redeploy with az deployment group create in the default mode. Is the workspace deleted? If you want code to delete it, what should you use?
quiz.a: No — incremental mode leaves resources that aren't in the file untouched. Use a deployment stack with --action-on-unmanage deleteResources (or deleteAll) — why: complete mode is no longer recommended and is being gradually deprecated in favour of stacks.

quiz.q: Before a production change, Pak Budi wants to see exactly what will happen. Which command do you run, and what does a ~ in front of a resource mean?
quiz.a: az deployment group what-if (or az deployment group create --confirm-with-what-if); ~ means the resource exists and will be modified, with the changing properties listed underneath — why: what-if previews the change without making it.

quiz.q: A company runs on Azure but also wants the same tool and workflow to manage its DNS at another provider and its GitHub repositories. Bicep or Terraform?
quiz.a: Terraform — why: Bicep only deploys Azure resources, while Terraform has providers for many clouds and SaaS products (at the cost of a state file you must store and protect).

quiz.q: Pak Budi wants nobody except the deployment pipeline to be able to delete the production virtual network created from the Bicep file. What do you use, and why not a CanNotDelete lock?
quiz.a: Deploy it as a deployment stack with --deny-settings-mode denyDelete and the pipeline's identity in --deny-settings-excluded-principals — why: a lock applies to everyone, including the pipeline, while stack deny settings can exempt named principals and are managed together with the code.

takeaways: Infrastructure as code turns your environment into reviewable, repeatable files; declarative deployments are idempotent, so redeploying is safe.
Bicep is a concise language that compiles to ARM JSON with day-one support for every Azure API; Terraform adds multi-cloud reach at the cost of a state file.
A Bicep file is parameters, variables, resources with symbolic names, outputs, and optionally modules, loops and conditions; references like nsgWeb.id create implicit dependencies.
Deploy in incremental mode, always preview with what-if, and remember the file describes the complete desired state of each resource.

Deployment stacks manage a group of resources as a unit, delete what leaves the file and protect resources with deny settings; together with template specs and Azure Policy they replace Azure Blueprints.

lab.title: Nineteen lunches of clicks in one file
lab.text:
What you'll build

For nineteen lunches, Nusantara Retail's cloud grew one click and one command at a time. Dewi now wants a fresh test copy of the storefront basics every Monday and nothing left running on Friday, and Ibu Sari wants to be sure nobody deletes production by accident. In this lab you finish a Bicep file that describes a storage account, a virtual network with two subnets and a network security group, and a Log Analytics workspace. You compile it, preview it with what-if, deploy it, change one parameter and deploy it again. Finally you deploy the same file as a deployment stack that refuses deletes — and remove everything at once by deleting the stack.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). For Task 6 you need Owner (or Contributor plus Azure Deployment Stack Owner): creating a stack with deny settings needs a permission that Contributor alone doesn't have. In your own subscription you are Owner.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install: the Azure CLI and the Bicep CLI are already there.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/20-infrastructure-as-code-bicep
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 20)

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist — very little here, because an empty storage account and a workspace that receives no data cost almost nothing. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create the resource group and build the starter

The Bicep file deploys into a resource group, so create that first. Then make your own working copy of the starter file and compile it.

ensure_rg "$RG" 20
cp starter/main.bicep main.bicep      # only the first time: this overwrites your copy
az bicep build --file main.bicep
ls main.*

az bicep build transpiles Bicep into an ARM JSON template, main.json, and prints nothing when there are no errors or warnings (the very first run may install the Bicep CLI for the Azure CLI, which takes a few seconds). Open main.json with code main.json and scroll through it — this is what Resource Manager receives, and why you'd rather write Bicep. Then read main.bicep from the top: four parameters (location defaults to the resource group's region, suffix to uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)), two variables (allTags adds the environment to the tags), a finished storage account, two outputs, and four EXERCISE blocks for you.

Checkpoint: az bicep build finishes without an error, and ls main.* shows main.bicep and main.json.

Task 2 · Complete the four exercises

Open your copy in the Cloud Shell editor with code main.bicep (Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Q closes), or in VS Code with the Bicep extension if you want IntelliSense. Paste each block below directly under its EXERCISE comment block, then run az bicep build --file main.bicep to check your work after every exercise. Stuck? Compare with solution/main.bicep.

Exercise 1 — the network security group. A rule is an object with a name and its own properties:

resource nsgWeb 'Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups@2024-05-01' = {
  name: 'nsg-web'
  location: location
  tags: allTags
  properties: {
    securityRules: [
      {
        name: 'Allow-HTTP-From-Internet'
        properties: {
          priority: 100
          direction: 'Inbound'
          access: 'Allow'
          protocol: 'Tcp'
          sourceAddressPrefix: 'Internet'
          sourcePortRange: '*'
          destinationAddressPrefix: '*'
          destinationPortRange: '80'
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

Exercise 2 — the virtual network. Define the subnets inside the virtual network, as the docs recommend, so a redeploy never tries to remove them. nsgWeb.id is a symbolic reference: it creates the dependency, so Bicep deploys the NSG first. defaultOutboundAccess: false makes both subnets private (no default outbound internet access).

resource vnet 'Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks@2024-05-01' = {
  name: 'vnet-nusa-iac'
  location: location
  tags: allTags
  properties: {
    addressSpace: {
      addressPrefixes: [
        '10.20.0.0/16'
      ]
    }
    subnets: [
      {
        name: 'snet-web'
        properties: {
          addressPrefix: '10.20.1.0/24'
          defaultOutboundAccess: false
          networkSecurityGroup: {
            id: nsgWeb.id
          }
        }
      }
      {
        name: 'snet-app'
        properties: {
          addressPrefix: '10.20.2.0/24'
          defaultOutboundAccess: false
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

Exercise 3 — the Log Analytics workspace. String interpolation (${suffix}) builds a name that is the same on every redeploy to this resource group:

resource logs 'Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces@2023-09-01' = {
  name: 'log-nusa-${suffix}'
  location: location
  tags: allTags
  properties: {
    sku: {
      name: 'PerGB2018'
    }
    retentionInDays: 30
  }
}

Exercise 4 — the outputs. Outputs hand values back to you or to the next step of a pipeline. Never output a secret:

output vnetId string = vnet.id
output webSubnetId string = vnet.properties.subnets[0].id
output logAnalyticsWorkspaceId string = logs.id

Build once more and count what the file now declares:

az bicep build --file main.bicep
grep -c '^resource ' main.bicep
grep -c '^output ' main.bicep

Tip: Working in VS Code with the Bicep extension? Hover over nsgWeb.id to see its type, and open the Bicep visualizer (the icon at the top right of the editor) to see the dependency between the NSG and the virtual network drawn for you.

Checkpoint: the build prints no errors, and the two grep commands print 4 (resources) and 5 (outputs).

Task 3 · Preview the deployment with what-if

Before anything changes in Azure, ask for a preview. What-if compiles the file, sends it to Resource Manager and compares it with what exists — nothing is created.

az deployment group what-if \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --template-file main.bicep

Every resource is marked + (create), with the properties it will get listed underneath. The last line is the summary:

Resource changes: 4 to create.

Checkpoint: what-if lists nsg-web, vnet-nusa-iac, a log-nusa-… workspace and a stiac… storage account, all with +, and the summary says 4 to create.

Task 4 · Deploy, then deploy the same file again

Deploy for real. A named deployment is easy to find later in the resource group's deployment history. It takes about one to two minutes.

az deployment group create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name lab20-main \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --query "properties.outputs" \
  --output jsonc

The output is the five outputs from your file. Now look at what was created and how it was tagged:

az resource list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, type:type, costCenter:tags.costCenter, environment:tags.environment}" \
  --output table

Here is the point of declarative code: run what-if again, then deploy again.

az deployment group what-if --resource-group "$RG" --template-file main.bicep
az deployment group create --resource-group "$RG" --name lab20-main-again --template-file main.bicep --output none
az deployment group list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, state:properties.provisioningState, timestamp:properties.timestamp}" --output table

What-if now marks the resources = (no change). The second deployment succeeds and changes nothing: the file is idempotent. What-if can show some noise — for example a ~ on the virtual network for a property Azure filled in with a default — so read the property lines, not only the summary.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open Resource groups › rg-lunch20-<suffix> › Settings › Deployments. Each deployment keeps its template, its parameter values and its outputs.

Checkpoint: four resources, each with costCenter = retail-lab and environment = lab, and two deployments (lab20-main and lab20-main-again) with the state Succeeded.

Task 5 · Change a parameter and watch what-if say "modify"

Dewi wants this copy to be marked as a test environment. You don't touch the resources — you change the input:

az deployment group what-if \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters environment=test

Now each resource is marked ~ (modify), and the change is listed underneath:

~ tags.environment: "lab" => "test"

Deploy the change, and let the CLI show the what-if result once more and ask before it deploys. Answer y:

az deployment group create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name lab20-environment-test \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters environment=test \
  --confirm-with-what-if

The @allowed decorator protects the input as well: try --parameters environment=dev with what-if, and Resource Manager rejects the value before anything is changed.

Checkpoint: az resource list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].tags.environment" --output tsv prints test four times.

Task 6 · Deploy it as a deployment stack with DenyDelete

A normal deployment forgets its resources as soon as it finishes. A deployment stack remembers them, can delete what leaves the file, and can protect them with deny settings. Deploy the same file as a stack. The resources already exist, so the stack simply takes them over. It takes about two minutes:

az stack group create \
  --name stack-nusa-iac \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters environment=test \
  --action-on-unmanage deleteResources \
  --deny-settings-mode denyDelete \
  --yes \
  --output none

az stack group show --name stack-nusa-iac --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "{state: provisioningState, denySettings: denySettings.mode, managedResources: resources[].id}" \
  --output jsonc

--action-on-unmanage deleteResources means: delete a resource when it leaves the file or when the stack is deleted. --deny-settings-mode denyDelete puts a deny assignment on every managed resource. Now act like someone who wants to "tidy up" the storage account:

STORAGE=$(az storage account list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[0].name" --output tsv)
az storage account delete --name "$STORAGE" --resource-group "$RG" --yes

The delete is refused with an error like this, even though you are an Owner:

(DenyAssignmentAuthorizationFailed) The client '…' with object id '…' has permission to perform action
'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete' on scope '…'; however, the access is denied because of the deny
assignment with name '…' and Id '…' at scope '…'.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open Resource groups › rg-lunch20-<suffix> › Settings › Deployment stacks › stack-nusa-iac to see the managed resources and the deny settings, and Access control (IAM) › Deny assignments to see the assignment the stack created. Try deleting the storage account there too.

Checkpoint: the stack shows denyDelete and lists your resources as managed, and the storage account still exists after the failed delete. Now run bash verify.sh (see Verify your work) — Task 7 removes everything it checks.

Task 7 · Delete the stack, and everything with it

When the test week is over, one command removes the stack, its deny assignment and every resource it manages. It takes a few minutes:

az stack group delete \
  --name stack-nusa-iac \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --action-on-unmanage deleteResources \
  --yes

az resource list --resource-group "$RG" --output table

The resource group is empty now — but the file still describes everything. Run the az stack group create command from Task 6 again if you want to see the whole environment come back in a couple of minutes, then delete the stack again.

Checkpoint: az resource list prints nothing and az stack group list --resource-group "$RG" --output table shows no stacks.

Break it and fix it

Typos in symbolic names are the most common Bicep mistake — and the cheapest one to catch. In your main.bicep, change the NSG reference in the virtual network from nsgWeb.id to nsgWbe.id, save, and build:

az bicep build --file main.bicep

Symptom: the build fails before Azure sees anything, with an error that names the file, the line and the column:

main.bicep(…) : Error BCP082: The name "nsgWbe" does not exist in the current context. Did you mean "nsgWeb"?

Hint and fix

The error is about the symbolic name — the name the file uses for the NSG — not about the Azure resource name nsg-web. Change nsgWbe back to nsgWeb and build again: no output means no errors. In VS Code the Bicep extension underlines the typo as you type and offers the fix. If a name isn't close enough to an existing symbol, you get BCP057: The name "…" does not exist in the current context. instead.

Verify your work

Run this at the end of Task 6, while the stack still exists:

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. It confirms the storage account, the virtual network with snet-web (with an NSG that allows port 80 in) and snet-app, the Log Analytics workspace, the costCenter and environment tags on every resource, and a deployment stack with denyDelete and deleteResources that manages the storage account. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. Already finished Task 7? Run the az stack group create command from Task 6 again, then verify.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes any deployment stack that is left in rg-lunch20-<suffix> together with the resources it manages (the deny assignment would otherwise block the deletes), and then the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes. The Log Analytics workspace stays recoverable for 14 days (soft delete) at no cost; your local main.bicep and main.json are just files in your clone.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Error BCP018: Expected the "}" character at this location. | A missing or extra brace or bracket after pasting | Compare the block with solution/main.bicep; every { and [ needs its partner
BCP037: The property "adressPrefix" is not allowed on objects of type … | A misspelled property name | Fix the spelling; the message lists the permissible properties
Error BCP082 or BCP057: The name "…" does not exist in the current context. | A typo in a symbolic name, or an exercise that refers to a resource you haven't added yet | See Break it and fix it; add the exercises in order
az: 'stack' is not in the 'az' command group. | An old Azure CLI (deployment stacks need 2.61 or later) | Use Cloud Shell, or run az upgrade
does not have authorization to perform action 'Microsoft.Resources/deploymentStacks/manageDenySetting/action' | You are Contributor, not Owner | Ask for Owner or Azure Deployment Stack Owner on the resource group, or use --deny-settings-mode none and read along
StorageAccountAlreadyTaken | Someone else uses the same storage account name — only likely if you passed your own suffix | Remove the suffix parameter, or choose a more unusual one
(InvalidTemplate) Deployment template validation failed: 'The provided value 'dev' for the template parameter 'environment' is not valid. | A value that @allowed doesn't list | Use lab, test or prod
What-if shows ~ for the virtual network although you changed nothing | What-if noise: Azure filled in a default value | Read the property lines; if they are defaults you never set, nothing really changes
Deleting the storage account in Task 6 succeeds | The stack was created without deny settings, or you deleted before the stack finished | Recreate the stack with --deny-settings-mode denyDelete (Task 6)
cleanup.sh or az group delete fails with DenyAssignmentAuthorizationFailed | A stack with deny settings still protects resources in the group | Delete the stack first (Task 7); cleanup.sh does this for you — run it again
(ResourceGroupNotFound) Resource group 'rg-lunch20-…' could not be found. | Task 1 was skipped, or cleanup.sh already ran | Run ensure_rg "$RG" 20 from Task 1

Stretch goals

- Move the test settings into a parameter file: create main.test.bicepparam with using 'main.bicep' and param environment = 'test', then deploy with --parameters main.test.bicepparam.
- Delete the Log Analytics workspace resource from main.bicep and run the az stack group create command from Task 6 again. Because of deleteResources, the stack deletes the workspace that left the file. With detachAll it would stay as an unmanaged resource.
- Add a tag by hand (az tag update --resource-id <id> --operation Merge --tags owner=rizky) — DenyDelete allows writes — then redeploy the stack and watch the file win: the extra tag disappears.
- Create several blob containers with a loop ([for name in containerNames: …]) as child resources of the storage account.
- Replace the storage account with the Azure Verified Module for storage accounts (br/public:avm/res/storage/storage-account:<version>); look up the current version in the module index.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep) — though this lab is about doing it with Bicep:

1. One Bicep file that deploys into rg-lunch20-<suffix>, with parameters for the location (default: the resource group's region), a name suffix (default: uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)), the environment (lab, test or prod) and the tags. No hard-coded region.
2. A Standard_LRS StorageV2 storage account; a virtual network with the subnets snet-web and snet-app, where snet-web uses a network security group that allows inbound TCP 80 from the internet; and a Log Analytics workspace.
3. Every resource tagged costCenter=retail-lab and environment=<the environment parameter>.
4. Outputs for the storage account name, the virtual network ID, the web subnet ID and the workspace ID (not checked by verify.sh).
5. Deploy it as a deployment stack with deny settings mode denyDelete and action on unmanage deleteResources, and show that deleting the storage account is refused.

Then run bash verify.sh while the stack exists. Stuck? Peek at solution/main.bicep and solution.sh, or switch to Guided mode.
